lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Supervised application: secure storage of sensitive documents

objective: Learners talk with a trusted adult about what secure document storage would realistically look like in their own household, so they leave with an actual plan rather than a hypothetical one, while never naming or handling the sensitive contents of any real document.
scenario: With a trusted adult, the learner discusses and records, at a category level only, where important documents could be kept securely in their household (for example, a locked drawer, a folder a guardian keeps, or a password-protected note that itself contains no real passwords) and confirms the plan is one the household could actually use.
safetyNotes: The conversation covers where documents would be kept, never their actual contents, numbers, or any password or PIN.
No password, PIN, or account credential is ever written down as part of this task, even as an example.
If a household genuinely has no secure storage option right now, naming that gap honestly is an acceptable outcome — the task is the conversation and the honest plan, not a guaranteed 'yes.'

simulationAlternative.description: If no adult is available for this conversation today, the learner instead designs a secure-storage plan for a fictional household using the same categories and criteria, and explains what they would ask a real adult about when one is available.

tasks.directions: Before the conversation, list what you think 'secure' means for a physical document versus a digital one.

prompts.text: In your own words, what makes storage 'secure' for a paper document, and what makes storage 'secure' for a digital one? They don't have to be the same answer.

tasks.directions: With your adult, talk through where important documents could realistically be kept in your household and record the plan by category.

prompts.text: I talked with an adult about where physical documents could be kept securely.
I talked with an adult about where digital records or accounts could be kept securely, without writing down any actual password.
My adult confirmed the plan is realistic for our household, or we honestly named a gap instead.

tasks.directions: Summarize the plan in your own words.

prompts.text: In your own words, summarize the secure-storage plan you and your adult discussed, including any category that is still unresolved.
Was there a category that turned out to be more complicated to discuss than you expected? What made it complicated?

remediation: If the learner's summary describes an idealized plan that does not match what the adult actually confirmed during the conversation, reteach by having the learner re-ask the adult to state the plan back in their own words first, then revise the written summary to match what was actually agreed.
extension: Have the learner identify one document category not on the provided checklist that applies to their situation, and add it to the plan with the adult's input.
